title: Outer Space from the Ground Up
description: A first look at space for someone starting from zero. The course begins with what you can see from your own backyard and works outward: the Moon and planets, the Sun, the stars, and the galaxies beyond. Distances and sizes are built up with everyday comparisons before any numbers are introduced. You will finish able to find major objects in the night sky and explain how astronomers know what they know.
objectives: Find the Moon’s phase, at least two planets and three bright stars or constellations in the night sky.
Explain day, night, seasons and lunar phases using models you can make at home.
Describe the planets of the solar system and how they differ.
Explain what stars are and how they live and die, in plain language.
Describe the scale of the universe using comparisons and light-travel time.

preface:
This book is about space, and it starts right where you are standing. You do not need to know anything yet. You only need to look up.

We begin with what your own eyes can see (the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars) and go a little farther out in each chapter, past the planets, out to other stars and on to other galaxies. To make the huge distances feel real, we will build one scale model and keep extending it: in it, the Sun is a ball the size of a bowling ball and Earth is a peppercorn across a football field.

You will also keep a sky diary, a few lines about what you see on clear nights. Every fact in this book is checked, and every big claim comes with the story of how someone found it out.

runningExamples.name: The pocket scale model
runningExamples.use: One consistent model used all book: if the Sun were a ball about 20 cm (8 inches) across, Earth would be a peppercorn about 24 m (26 yards) away (Guy Ottewell's Thousand-Yard Model). Extend it chapter by chapter.

runningExamples.name: Your sky diary
runningExamples.use: A simple observing log the reader keeps from Chapter 1: the Moon's shape, a bright planet, a star's color.

runningExamples.name: The Moon
runningExamples.use: The nearest world, revisited as the book moves outward.

conventions: Simple words; define every term the first time; never talk down.
Give big numbers with a comparison to something familiar.
Say what you can see with the naked eye, with binoculars, and only with telescopes.
